source_text: Sed quotiens de nativitate contenditur, omnes, qui respuunt eam ut praeiudicantem de carnis in Christo veritate, ipsum deum volunt negare esse natum, quia dixerit: Quae mihi mater, et qui mihi fratres? Audiat igitur et Apelles quid iam responsum sit a nobis Marcioni eo libello que evangelium ipsius provocavimus, considerandam scilicet materiam pronuntialionis istius. Primo quidem nunquam quisquam annuntiasset illi matrem et fratres eius foris stantes qui non certus esset et habere illum matrem et fratres et ipsos esse quos tunc nuntiabat, vel retro cognitos vel tunc ibidem compertos; licet propterea abstulerint haereses ista de evangelio, quod et creditum patrem eius Ioseph fabrum et matrem Mariam et fratres et sorores eius optime notos sibi esse dicebant qui mirabantur doctrinam eius. Sed temptandi gratia nuntiaverant ei matrem et fratres, quos non habebat. Hoc quidem scriptura non dicit, alias non tacens cum quid temptationis gratia factum est erga cum. Ecce, inquit, surrexit legis doctor temptans eum. Et alibi, Et accesserunt ad eum pharisaei temptantes eum. Quod nemo prohibebat hic quoque significari temptandi gratia factum. Non recipio quod extra scripturam de tuo infers. Dehinc materia temptationis debet subesse. Quid temptandum putaverint in illo? utique natusne esset an non? Si enim hoc negavit responsio eius, hoc captavit nuntiatio temptatoris. Sed nulla temptatio, tendens ad agnitionem eius de quo dubitando temptat, ita subito procedit, ut non ante praecedat quaestio quae dubitationem inferens cogat temptationem. Porro si nusquam de nativitate Christi volutatum est, quid tu argumentaris voluisse illos per temptationem sciscitari quod nunquam produxerunt in quaestionem? Eo adicimus etiam, si temptandus esset de nativitate, non utique hoc modo temptaretur, earum personarum annuntiatione quae poterant etiam nato Christo non fuisse. Omnes nascimur, et tamen non omnes aut fratres habemus aut matrem. Adhuc potest et patrem magis habere quam matrem, et avunculos magis quam fratras. Adeo non competit temptatio nativitatis, quam licebat et sine matris lot sine fratrum nominatione constare. Facilius plane est ut certi illum ut matrem et fratres habere divinitatem potius temptaverint cius quam nativitatem, an intas agens sciret quid foris esset, mendacio petitus praesentiae annuntiatas eorum, qui in praesentia non erant. Nisi quod sic vacuisset temptationis ingenium. Poterat enim evenire, ut quos illi nuntiabunt foris stare, ille cos sciret abrentes esse, vel valetudinis vel negotii vel peregrinationis notae iam necessitate. Nemo temptat eo modo quo sciat posse se ruborem temptationis referre. Nulla igitur materia temptationis competente liberatur simplicitas nuntiationis, quod vere mater et fratres eius super venissent. Sed quae ratio responsi matrem et fratres ad praesens negantis discat etiam Apelles. Fratres domini non crediderant in illum, sicut evangelio ante Marcionem edito continetur. Mater aeque non demonstratur adhaesisse illi, cum Marthae et Mariae aliae in commercio eius frequententur. Hoc denique in loco apparet incredulitas corum: cum Iesus doceret viam vitae, cum dei regnum praedicaret, cum languoribus et vitiis medendis operaretur, extraneis defixis in illum tam proximi aberant. Denique superveniunt et foris subsistunt, nec introsunt, non computantes scilicet quid intus ageretur, nec sustinent saltem, quasi necessarius aliquid afferrent co quod ille cum maxime agebat, sed amplius interpellant et a tanto opere revocatum volunt. Oro te, Apelle, vel tu, Marcion, si forte tabula ludens vel de histrionibus aut aurigis contendeus tali nuntio avocareris, nonne dixisses: Quae mihi mater, aut qui fratres? Deum praedicans et probans Christus, legem et prophetas adimplens, tanti retro aevi caliginem dispargens, indigue usus est hoc dicto ad percutiendam incredulitatem foris stantium vel ad excutiendam importunitatem ab opere revocantium? Ceterum ad negandam nativitatem alius fuisset ei locus et tempus et ordo sermonis, non eius qui posset pronuntiari etiam ab eo cui et mater esset et fratres. Cum indignatio parentes negat, non negat, sed obiurgat. Denique potiores fecit alios, et meritum praelationis ostendens, audientiam scilicet verbi, demonstrat qua condicione negaverit matrem et fratres. Qua enim alios sibi adoptavit qui ei adhaerebant, ea abnegavit illos qui ab eo adsistebant. Solet etiam adimplere Christus quod alios docet. Quale ergo erat si docens non tanti facere matrem aut patrem aut fratres quanti dei verbum ipse dei verbum annuntiata matre et fraternitate desereret? Negavit itaque parentes quomodo docuit negandos pro dei opere. Sed et alias figura est synagogae in matre abiuncta et Indaeorum in fratribus incredulis. Foris erat in illis IsraÃ«l, discipuli autem novi intus audientes et credentes cohaerentes Christo ecclesiam deliniabant, quam potiorem matrem et digniorem fraternitatem recusato carnali genere nuncupavit. Eodem sensu denique et illi exclamationi respondit, non matris uterum et ubera negans, sed feliciores designans qui verbum dei audiunt.
thought_title: The announcement of mother and brothers was a test, not a denial of birth
orientation: Tertullian is answering Apelles and Marcion, who use Christ's words 'Who is my mother, and who are my brothers?' to deny that Christ was truly born.
pass_a_gloss: But as often as there is dispute about birth, all who reject it as prejudging the truth of the flesh in Christ want to deny that God himself was born, because he said: Who is mother to me, and who are brothers to me? Let Apelles therefore also hear what has already been answered by us to Marcion in that little book in which we challenged his own gospel, namely that the matter of that announcement must be considered. First indeed no one would ever have announced to him his mother and his brothers standing outside who was not certain both that he had a mother and brothers and that they themselves were the ones whom he was then announcing, either known before or discovered then in that same place; although for this reason those heresies have removed these things from the gospel, because they were saying that his father Joseph the carpenter and his mother Mary and his brothers and his sisters were very well known to them, who were marveling at his teaching. But they had announced to him, for the sake of testing, a mother and brothers whom he did not have. This indeed the scripture does not say, although elsewhere it is not silent when something was done for the sake of testing against him. Behold, it says, a teacher of the law rose up testing him. And elsewhere, And the Pharisees came to him testing him. What no one was preventing should also be indicated here as done for the sake of testing. I do not accept what you bring in from outside the scripture. Next the matter of the testing ought to underlie it. What did they think should be tested in him? Surely whether he had been born or not? For if his answer denied this, the announcement of the tempter aimed at this. But no testing, tending toward recognition of him about whom it tests by doubting, proceeds so suddenly that a question does not first precede which, bringing in doubt, forces the testing. Furthermore if nowhere was there discussion about the birth of Christ, why do you argue that they wanted to inquire by testing what they never brought into question? To this we add also, if he had to be tested about birth, he would not at any rate be tested in this way, by the announcement of those persons who could have been absent even though Christ had been born. We are all born, and yet not all of us have either brothers or a mother. Still one can have a father rather than a mother, and uncles rather than brothers. So the testing of birth does not fit, which could stand even without the naming of a mother or of brothers. It is quite easier that, being certain that he had a mother and brothers, they rather tested his divinity than his birth, whether acting inside he knew what was outside, sought by a lie about the presence of those announced, who were not present. Except that in this way the cleverness of the testing would have been empty. For it could happen that those whom they announced as standing outside, he knew to be absent, by the already known necessity of health or business or travel. No one tests in a way by which he knows he can bring back the shame of the testing. Therefore since no matter of testing fits, the simplicity of the announcement is freed, that truly his mother and his brothers had come up. But let Apelles also learn what the reason of the answer was, denying mother and brothers for the present. The brothers of the Lord had not believed in him, as is contained in the gospel published before Marcion. His mother likewise is not shown to have clung to him, while other Marthas and Marys are frequented in his company. This finally appears in this place, their unbelief: while Jesus was teaching the way of life, while he was preaching the kingdom of God, while he was working at healing weaknesses and faults, with strangers fixed on him, those so close were absent. Finally they come up and stand outside, and do not enter, not reckoning of course what was being done inside, nor do they even wait, as if they were bringing something necessary to what he was especially doing, but rather they interrupt and want him called away from so great a work. I ask you, Apelles, or you, Marcion, if by chance playing at dice or contending about actors or charioteers you were called away by such a message, would you not have said: Who is mother to me, or who are brothers? Christ, preaching and proving God, fulfilling the law and the prophets, scattering the darkness of so long an age, did he use this saying unworthily to strike the unbelief of those standing outside or to shake off the importunity of those calling him away from the work? Otherwise for denying birth there would have been another place and time and order of speech for him, not one which could be uttered even by him who had both a mother and brothers. When indignation denies parents, it does not deny, but rebukes. Finally he made others more important, and showing the merit of the preference, namely the hearing of the word, he shows on what condition he denied mother and brothers. For by the same thing by which he adopted others for himself who clung to him, he disowned those who stood apart from him. Christ is also accustomed to fulfill what he teaches others. What sort of thing therefore would it be if, teaching that mother or father or brothers are not to be valued as much as the word of God, he himself, the word of God, should desert the announced mother and brotherhood? Therefore he denied parents in the way he taught they must be denied for the work of God. But also in another way there is a figure of the synagogue in the mother set apart and of the Jews in the unbelieving brothers. Israel was outside in them, but the new disciples inside hearing and believing and clinging to Christ were sketching out the church, which he named a more important mother and a worthier brotherhood, the fleshly kindred having been refused. In the same sense finally he also answered that exclamation, not denying the womb and breasts of his mother, but designating as more blessed those who hear the word of God.

pass_b_english: But whenever the question of birth is raised, all who reject it as prejudging the truth of the flesh in Christ want to deny that God himself was born, because he said, “Who is mother to me, and who are brothers to me?” (Matthew 12:48). So let Apelles also hear what I have already answered to Marcion in that book in which I challenged his own gospel: the context of that announcement must be considered.

First of all, no one would ever have announced to him that his mother and brothers were standing outside unless he was certain that he had a mother and brothers, and that these were the very people he was announcing—either known to him before or discovered then and there. Though these heresies have cut this passage out of the gospel for that very reason, because those who marveled at his teaching were saying that his supposed father Joseph the carpenter, his mother Mary, and his brothers and sisters were very well known to them.

But, you say, they announced his mother and brothers to him for the sake of testing him, whom he did not have. Scripture does not say this, though elsewhere it does not keep silent when something was done to test him. “Look,” it says, “a teacher of the law stood up to test him” (Luke 10:25). And elsewhere, “The Pharisees came to him to test him” (Matthew 19:3). Nothing prevented it from also being stated here that this was done in order to test him. But I do not accept what you bring in from outside Scripture.

Next, there must be a reason for the testing. What did they think they were testing in him? Surely whether he had been born or not. For if his answer denied it, the announcement of the testers was aiming at that. But no test that aims at discovering something about a person it doubts proceeds so abruptly that a question does not come first—a question that introduces the doubt and prompts the test.

Furthermore, if the question of Christ's birth was never discussed anywhere, why do you argue that they wanted to find out through a test what they never brought into question? I add this too: even if he had to be tested about his birth, he would not have been tested in this way, by announcing persons who might not have existed even if Christ had been born. We are all born, and yet not all of us have brothers or a mother. A man can have a father rather than a mother, and uncles rather than brothers. So a test about birth does not fit here, since birth could be established without naming a mother or brothers.

It is far more plausible that, being certain he had a mother and brothers, they were testing his divinity rather than his birth—whether he knew what was outside while he was inside, when they falsely announced the presence of people who were not present. Except that this would have made the test pointless. For it could have happened that the people they announced as standing outside were known to him to be away, kept away by illness, business, or travel. No one tests in a way that he knows could bring him the shame of a failed test.

Since no reason for testing fits, the plain meaning of the announcement stands: his mother and brothers had truly come. But let Apelles also learn the reason for the answer of the one who denied his mother and brothers at that moment. The Lord's brothers had not believed in him, as is contained in the gospel published before Marcion. Likewise his mother is not shown to have stayed close to him, while other women—Martha and Mary—are found in his company.

In this passage their unbelief is finally apparent. While Jesus was teaching the way of life, while he was preaching the kingdom of God, while he was working to heal sicknesses and defects, with strangers fixed on him, those so close to him were absent. Finally they arrive and stand outside, and do not enter—evidently not considering what was happening inside. They do not even wait, as if they were bringing something necessary to what he was doing at that very moment, but they interrupt and want to call him away from so great a work.

Tell me, Apelles—or you, Marcion—if you were playing a board game or competing about actors or charioteers and were called away by such an announcement, would you not have said, “Who is mother to me, or who are brothers?” Christ was preaching and proving God, fulfilling the law and the prophets, scattering the darkness of so long an age—was it unworthy of him to use this saying to strike the unbelief of those standing outside, or to shake off the importunity of those calling him away from his work?

Besides, to deny his birth there would have been another place, another time, another order of speech—not a saying that could also be spoken by someone who did have a mother and brothers. When indignation denies parents, it does not deny them; it rebukes them. Finally, he made others more important, and by showing the ground of his preference—namely, hearing the word—he shows on what condition he denied mother and brothers. For by the very thing by which he adopted others who clung to him, he disowned those who stood apart from him.

Christ also usually fulfills what he teaches others. What kind of example would it be if, while teaching that mother or father or brothers are not to be valued as highly as the Word, he himself, when his mother and brothers were announced, abandoned the Word? So he denied his parents in the way he taught they must be denied for the work of God.

But there is also another meaning: the mother set apart is a figure of the synagogue, and the unbelieving brothers a figure of the Jews. In them Israel was outside, but the new disciples inside, hearing and believing and clinging to Christ, were sketching out the church—which he called a more excellent mother and a worthier brotherhood, rejecting the fleshly family. In the same sense he answered that exclamation too, not denying his mother's womb and breasts, but declaring more blessed those who hear the Word (Luke 11:28).
